_what: Published slice/image-level vs patient/exam-level rank inversions located 2026-07-29. Every number below was read from the source named in 'source_url' and is reproduced verbatim from a table or leaderboard.
_search_limitation: WebSearch was unavailable for the whole session (API error). Evidence was gathered via Europe PMC full-text search (10 queries -> 979 unique open-access PMCIDs, 821 with retrievable fullTextXML), an automated paired-table rank-inversion scan over those 821, the arXiv API, and direct fetches of challenge leaderboards. Kaggle/GitHub solution write-ups and non-indexed grey literature were therefore NOT systematically searched.

cases.kind: challenge leaderboard, same submissions scored at two units
cases.citation: CAMELYON16 official public leaderboards; Ehteshami Bejnordi B, et al. JAMA 2017;318(22):2199-2210.
cases.fine_unit: lesion (FROC = mean sensitivity at 1/4,1/2,1,2,4,8 FP per WSI)
cases.headline: Top-5 membership changes. HMS/MGH Method 1 is 3rd by slide AUC (0.9650) and 6th by lesion FROC (0.5963); HMS/MGH Method 2 is 8th by AUC (0.9082) and 3rd by FROC (0.7289). The two methods from the same group reverse order between units.
cases.second_headline: On the Apr-1-deadline top-five boards the SETS differ: Radboud UMC (DIAG) is 2nd on the lesion board (0.5748) and absent from the slide top-five; 'Independent participant, Germany' is 3rd on the slide board (0.8654) and absent from the lesion top-five.
verbatim_quotes: Public Leaderboard 1 - Whole-slide-image classification ... Evaluation 1: Teams are ranked based on area under ROC curve (AUC).

Public Leaderboard 2 - Tumor localization ... Evaluation 2: The detection/localization performance is summarized using Free Response Operating Characteristic (FROC) curves. The final score is defined as the average sensitivity at 6 predefined false positive rates: 1/4, 1/2, 1, 2, 4, and 8 FPs per whole slide image.
caveats: The metric changes with the unit (AUC vs FROC) because AUC is not definable at lesion level; unit and metric are confounded, though the confound is entailed by the unit change.
2D pathology WSI, not volumetric CT/MRI; the fine unit is a lesion, not a slice.
Test set n=129 WSI (49 positive). The leaderboard publishes no confidence intervals, so most reorderings cannot be separated from sampling noise from the published numbers alone.

cases.kind: peer-reviewed benchmark study, same models at image and exam level
cases.citation: Islam NU, Gehlot S, Zhou Z, Gotway MB, Liang J. Seeking an Optimal Approach for Computer-Aided Pulmonary Embolism Detection. MLMI (MICCAI workshop) 2021; LNCS 12966:692-702.
cases.dataset: RSNA-STR Pulmonary Embolism CT (RSPED) -- the benchmark that ships image-level AND exam-level labels
cases.coarse_unit: exam-level mean AUC over 9 labels, conventional classification (Table 2)
verbatim_quotes: Although SeXception performed optimally for image-level classification (see Fig. 2), the same is not true for exam-level classification. There is no architecture that performs optimally across all labels, but overall, Xception shows the best AUC across nine labels.
Furthermore, SeXception is the optimal architecture for image-level classification, whereas Xception performs best for exam-level classification.
Based on our rigorous analysis, the optimal architectures for the tasks of image-level and exam-level classification are SeXception and Xception.
The features extracted by the models trained for image-level classification were helpful for exam-level classification. However, no model performed consistently best for all labels.
caveats: The exam-level number is a mean AUC over nine labels; the image-level number is a single PE label. Same benchmark and same models, but not literally the same metric.
Exam-level features are derived from the image-level models, so the two units are not independent estimators.

Image-level values carry run-to-run SDs (SeXception 0.9634+-0.0009, SeResNext50 0.9614+-0.0011, Xception 0.9607+-0.0007) but no subject-clustered CIs; exam-level Table 2 reports means over 10 runs with no dispersion at all.

cases.kind: single study, explicit dual-level evaluation, 5 architectures
cases.citation: Multi-Architecture Deep Learning for Early Alzheimer's Detection in MRI: Slice- and Scan-Level Analysis. Int J Environ Res Public Health 2026.
cases.coarse_unit: scan-level accuracy (627 test volumes), max-confidence aggregation
cases.headline: The slice-level rankings and scan-level rankings are strongly NEGATIVELY correlated. The slice-level best model is the scan-level worst.
verbatim_quotes: By evaluating performance at both slice-level and scan-level, we reveal that multi-slice aggregation affects architectures asymmetrically.

ConvNeXtV2-L achieved the best scan-level performance (91.07%), EfficientNetV2-L the highest slice-level accuracy (86.84%), and VGG19 balanced results (86.07%/88.52%). ConvNeXtV2-L and SwinV1-L exhibited scan-level improvements of 7.60% and 9.04% respectively, while EfficientNetV2-L experienced degradation of 2.66%, demonstrating that architectural selection and aggregation strategy are interdependent factors.
Most studies report either slice-level or scan-level performance without systematically investigating how aggregation affects different architectures.

EfficientNetV2-L unexpectedly showed degraded scan-level performance compared to slice-level results, suggesting the aggregation strategy may not effectively leverage this architecture's learned features.
caveats: SELECTION: 'Scan-level evaluation was conducted only for the five highest-performing models in slice-level classification.' Selecting on the slice axis truncates slice-level variance (range 0.0420) relative to scan-level variance (range 0.0654), which inflates apparent discordance. The tau of -0.600 is an upper bound on the effect.

AGGREGATION RULE: scan prediction is max-confidence over slices ('The slice achieving the highest maximum class probability determined the final scan-level classification'), an unusual rule that rewards high-variance confidence. Part of the reordering is a unit x aggregation-rule interaction, not a pure unit effect; the authors say so themselves.

LEAKAGE: split is scan-based, not subject-based -- 'Our scan-level splitting strategy did not enforce subject-level separation, meaning different visits from the same individual could appear across sets.' Neither number is a clean subject-level estimate.
No confidence intervals anywhere. MDPI IJERPH, 2026.
Their own Table 9 tabulates other studies' accuracies in a single comparison column with (I)/(P) unit flags -- direct evidence that the literature compares across units as if commensurable.

cases.kind: single study, 5 architectures, both units, same patient-level split
cases.citation: Guneri G, et al. A Vision Transformer-Based Deep Learning Framework for Patient-Level Classification of Acute Pancreatitis and Normal Pancreas Using Computed Tomography. Diagnostics 2026;16(8):1152.
cases.coarse_unit: patient-level accuracy (Table 3), majority vote over slices
verbatim_quotes: Although the Swin model achieved the highest accuracy rate in slice-level analysis, the ViT model was observed to exhibit more balanced and robust classification performance in patient-level evaluation.

In slice-level analysis, all models achieve high performance. Swin shows the highest accuracy (84.06%), and ViT revealed the most balanced performance with an F1-score of 82.90%. In the more clinically significant patient-level evaluation, the ViT model outperforms all others with an accuracy of 89.19%, an F1-score of 86.67%, and an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.946.
high slice-level accuracy rates do not guarantee the model's success in the clinical diagnostic process
cases.why_it_matters_most_for_our_trap: This is the ONLY located case that publishes patient-level CIs, and they show the inversion is not separable from noise: Table 7 gives ViT 89.19% [75.3-96.4] vs Swin 78.38% [62.8-89.2] on 37 test patients (21 normal, 16 AP). The intervals overlap heavily. The slice-level gap that put Swin first is 84.06 vs 83.75 = 0.31 points.
caveats: Test set is 37 patients. A published inversion with no ability to distinguish it from sampling variability.
Their own Table 4 (patient level WITH augmentation) reorders again: Swin and ViT tie at 85.14%, so the 'winner' also flips with a training-time choice.

adjacent_evidence.axis: SPLIT unit, not evaluation unit -- must not be conflated
adjacent_evidence.citation: Yagis E, et al. Effect of data leakage in brain MRI classification using 2D convolutional neural networks. Sci Rep 2021;11:22544.
adjacent_evidence.finding: Table 4, test accuracy for 3 CNNs x 6 datasets under slice-level vs subject-level splitting. The best architecture flips on 4 of 6 datasets; 9 of 18 architecture pairs reverse.
adjacent_evidence.note: Shows the unit-of-analysis choice reorders architectures on the SPLIT axis. Adjacent mechanism, strong citation, but it is leakage, not evaluation granularity.

adjacent_evidence.axis: the within-unit noise floor -- the comparator our analysis must beat
adjacent_evidence.citation: Maier-Hein L, et al. Why rankings of biomedical image analysis competitions should be interpreted with care. Nat Commun 2018;9:5217. (Author Correction: Nat Commun 2019;10:588.)
verbatim_quotes: the rank of an algorithm is generally not robust to a number of variables such as the test data used for validation, the ranking scheme applied and the observers that make the reference annotations
Even for relatively high values of Kendall's tau (b: tau = 0.74; c: tau = 0.85), critical changes in the ranking may occur
In some cases, almost all teams change their ranking position when the aggregation method is changed.
different observers produced different rankings in 15, 46, and 62% of the 13 pairwise comparisons between observers
adjacent_evidence.why_it_matters: Establishes that tau in the 0.74-0.85 range is already enough to change winners. Our CAMELYON16 unit-change tau of 0.754 sits inside that band, so the honest claim is that the unit change produces instability of the SAME ORDER as the aggregation-scheme instability already documented -- not larger. This is the paper we must cite when separating 'the unit changes the ranking' from 'the ranking is too noisy to be stable at all'.

negative_controls.citation: Discrimination between LGI1 antibody encephalitis and GABA-B receptor antibody encephalitis based on ResNet18. Vis Comput Ind Biomed Art 2023;6:17.
negative_controls.finding: Three architectures at BOTH units with DeLong tests. Slice AUC ResNet18 0.86 > ResNet50 0.74 > VGG16 0.67; patient AUC ResNet18 0.98 > ResNet50 0.86 > VGG16 0.73. Ranking is PRESERVED on AUC and on accuracy. A clean published counter-example: reporting both units does not always produce an inversion.

priority3_public_prediction_files.camelyon16: No raw per-team prediction files on the challenge site; unnecessary anyway, because the organisers themselves published both leaderboards.
priority3_public_prediction_files.rsna_str_pe: The public training set carries both image-level and exam-level labels, so a two-unit recomputation is possible on that split; Kaggle test labels are withheld and no published test-set prediction files were located.
priority3_public_prediction_files.limitation: WebSearch was unavailable, so Kaggle solution repositories and GitHub write-ups were not systematically searched. This arm is under-searched and should not be reported as a negative result.
